title: The Three Crowned Kings
description: An illustrated map of the early Tamil kingdoms, the Cheras, Cholas and Pandyas, from Iron Age burials and Ashoka’s edicts, through the Sangam poems and the Roman pepper trade, to the epics and the rediscovery of the poems.
mapLabel: Illustrated map of the Chera, Chola and Pandya kingdoms of the Sangam age, about 300 BCE to 300 CE
note: Based on excavations, inscriptions, the Sangam poems, Greek and Roman writers and Sri Lanka’s chronicle; each chapter says which it follows. Dates for the Sangam age, its kings and its poems are uncertain and debated, and the poems are poetry, not chronicles. The three kingdoms’ areas are painted loosely; borders shifted and many chiefs ruled on their own. The map is stylised and not to scale; Karur, Venni and Arikamedu are moved a little so their pins do not overlap.

steps.title: Urns by the Thamirabarani
steps.text: Upriver from Korkai, at Adichanallur on the Thamirabarani river, a hillside holds hundreds of burial urns. Excavated from 1899 and again from 2004, they held iron weapons and tools, bronze vessels, pottery and thin gold diadems. Their dates are debated, but most fall in the first millennium BCE, long before any written record of the south.
steps.today: Today: Adichanallur, Thoothukudi district, Tamil Nadu, India, with a site museum.

steps.title: A brick town on the Vaigai
steps.when: from about the 6th century BCE, by some estimates
steps.text: At Keezhadi, about 12 km south-east of Madurai, digs since 2015 have uncovered brick buildings, drains, ring wells, dice, beads and thousands of potsherds, some scratched with names in Tamil-Brahmi letters. The state’s archaeologists date the earliest layers to about the 6th century BCE; others argue for a later date, and the debate goes on.
steps.today: Today: the Keezhadi excavations and Keeladi Museum, Sivaganga district.

steps.title: The land of Pandaia
steps.text: Megasthenes, a Greek envoy at the Maurya court, heard of a southern kingdom called Pandaia. Later Greek writers repeat his story: Heracles gave it to his daughter Pandaia, women ruled it, and he searched the sea for pearls to adorn her. It is a legend, but the name is close to the Pandyas, whose port of Korkai fished pearls.
steps.today: Today: Korkai village, near the mouth of the Thamirabarani.

steps.title: Beyond Ashoka’s borders
steps.text: The Maurya emperor Ashoka never ruled the far south. His second rock edict, carved at Erragudi and other sites, names the peoples beyond his borders: the Cholas, the Pandyas, the Satiyaputras and the Keralaputras, as far as Sri Lanka. There, it says, he has provided medical care for people and animals, and planted herbs and dug wells.
steps.today: Today: the Ashokan rock edicts at Erragudi, Kurnool district, Andhra Pradesh.

steps.title: The first Tamil writing
steps.text: In caves at Mangulam, north-east of Madurai, stone beds were cut for Jain monks. Lines in Tamil-Brahmi above them, among the oldest Tamil inscriptions known, record the gift and name an officer of a Pandya king called Nedunjeliyan. Dozens of such cave inscriptions survive in the hills around Madurai; their exact dates are debated.
steps.today: Today: the Mangulam (Meenakshipuram) caves, Madurai district.

steps.title: A Chola king in Lanka
steps.text: Sri Lanka’s chronicle, the Mahavamsa, says a Tamil named Elara, from the Chola country, ruled Anuradhapura for 44 years. It praises his justice: a bell hung by his bed for anyone wronged. Prince Dutugamunu killed him in single combat, then honoured him with a monument and ordered all who passed it to show respect.
steps.today: Today: Anuradhapura, North Central Province, Sri Lanka.

steps.title: A league of Tamil kings
steps.text: In the Elephant Cave inscription at Udayagiri, King Kharavela of Kalinga boasts of breaking up a league of Tamil states that had stood for 113 years, and of receiving pearls and jewels from a Pandya king. The inscription is damaged, and both its date and these readings are debated, but it shows the southern kings acting together.
steps.today: Today: the Hathigumpha inscription, Udayagiri hills, Bhubaneswar, Odisha.

steps.title: The assemblies of poets
steps.text: A commentary of about the 8th century tells of three assemblies (sangams) of poets under the Pandya kings. The first met at a southern Madurai later swallowed by the sea, the second at Kapatapuram, also lost, and the third at Madurai itself, each lasting thousands of years. Historians treat this as tradition; the name Sangam stuck to the age.
steps.today: Today: Madurai, Tamil Nadu.

steps.title: Poems of love and war
steps.when: about the 1st to 3rd centuries CE, debated
steps.text: The Sangam poems survive in eight anthologies and ten long poems: 2,381 poems by 473 named poets, plus about a hundred unnamed. Love poems (akam) set each mood in a landscape, from mountains for union to the seashore for pining; poems of the outer world (puram) praise kings, battles and gifts. Most date from the early centuries CE.
steps.today: Today: the Eighteen Greater Texts (Patinenmelkanakku), read across the Tamil world.

steps.title: The Cheras of Vanci
steps.text: One anthology, the Ten Tens (Patirruppattu), praises Chera kings, among them Imayavaramban, ‘whose border is the Himalaya’, said to have carved the Chera bow on its peaks. Rock inscriptions at Pugalur, near Karur, name three generations of Chera kings, and the Chera bow appears on coins from the Amaravati river. Their capital, Vanci, is identified with Karur or Kodungallur.
steps.today: Today: Karur, on the Amaravati river, Tamil Nadu.

steps.title: Karikala at Venni
steps.text: At Venni, in the Kaveri delta, the young Chola king Karikala defeats the Chera and Pandya kings and eleven chieftains. The poems say the Chera king, wounded in the back, thought it a disgrace, and starved himself to death facing north. Karikala becomes the most famous Chola of the poems, though his dates are uncertain.
steps.today: Today: Kovil Venni, Tiruvarur district, Tamil Nadu.

steps.title: Puhar, the Kaveri’s port
steps.text: The long poem Pattinappalai pictures Karikala’s port at the Kaveri’s mouth: officers stamping the Chola tiger on goods, horses landed from overseas, pepper from the hills, pearls from the south and gold from the north. Tradition credits Karikala with banking the Kaveri, and the Grand Anicut (Kallanai) dam, still in use, is often attributed to him.
steps.today: Today: Poompuhar, Mayiladuthurai district, Tamil Nadu.

steps.title: The Pandya at Talaiyalanganam
steps.text: The Pandya king Nedunjeliyan, still young, beats the Chera and Chola kings and five chieftains at Talaiyalanganam. A poem in his own name vows that if he loses, poets may stop singing of him. The long poem Maduraikkanchi then describes his Madurai: its broad streets, temple festivals, and markets open by day and by night.
steps.today: Today: Thalaiyalangadu, Tiruvarur district; Madurai, Tamil Nadu.

steps.title: Avvaiyar and the gooseberry
steps.text: Kings were not the only patrons. Athiyaman, chief of Tagadur, gave the poet Avvaiyar a rare gooseberry (nellikkani) said to grant long life, keeping none for himself; she praised him in the poems and served as his envoy. A rock inscription at Jambai names him as ‘Satiyaputo’, the Satiyaputras of Ashoka’s edict.
steps.today: Today: Dharmapuri, Tamil Nadu; the Jambai inscription is in Kallakurichi district.

steps.title: Yavana ships at Muciri
steps.text: Using the monsoon winds to cross the open sea from Egypt’s Red Sea ports, ships reach the Chera coast. A Sangam poem describes the Yavanas’ fine ships coming to Muciri with gold and leaving laden with pepper. Yavana meant Greeks and later any westerner. Digs at Pattanam, north of Kochi, are thought to have found the port.
steps.today: Today: Pattanam, near Kodungallur, Ernakulam district, Kerala.

steps.title: Pliny counts the cost
steps.text: The Roman writer Pliny the Elder complains that India drains the empire of at least 50 million sesterces a year, for goods sold at a hundred times their cost. He names Muziris as India’s first market but warns of pirates and that ships must anchor far offshore. The Periplus, a sailors’ guide, lists it with the Pandya port of Nelcynda.
steps.today: Today: the Periyar river mouth, Kerala.

steps.title: The Muziris papyrus
steps.text: A papyrus now in Vienna records a loan for a voyage to Muziris. Its back lists the cargo of one returning ship, the Hermapollon: Gangetic nard, ivory and fine cloth, valued at millions of drachmas, with a quarter paid as tax on landing. It shows how large this trade was, and that pepper was not all the Tamil ports sold.
steps.today: Today: the papyrus is in the Austrian National Library, Vienna.

steps.title: Arikamedu’s beads
steps.when: about the 2nd century BCE to 2nd century CE
steps.text: On the east coast, near Puducherry, Mortimer Wheeler’s dig of 1945 found Italian red-glazed tableware (Arretine ware), wine and oil jars from the Mediterranean, and a workshop making glass and stone beads, traded across the Indian Ocean. Later digs showed the site was older than the Roman trade. It may be the Periplus’s port of Poduke.
steps.today: Today: Arikamedu, Ariyankuppam, Puducherry.

steps.title: Pearls and an embassy
steps.when: about 20 BCE to the 1st century CE
steps.text: The Periplus says the pearl fishery at Korkai belongs to the Pandya king and is worked by condemned criminals. The Greek geographer Strabo writes that a king called Pandion sent an embassy to the Roman emperor Augustus, though some sources name Porus instead. Roman gold and silver coins turn up in hoards across the south, many around Coimbatore.
steps.today: Today: Korkai; the sea has since retreated several kilometres.

steps.title: Kannagi’s anklet
steps.when: epic of about the 5th to 6th century, debated
steps.text: In the epic The Tale of the Anklet (Silappatikaram), Kovalan of Puhar is wrongly executed in Madurai for stealing the queen’s anklet. His wife Kannagi breaks her own anklet to show rubies, not the queen’s pearls; the Pandya king dies of shame and her anger burns Madurai. Tradition makes the poet, Ilango Adigal, a Chera prince.
steps.today: Today: Kannagi is worshipped as the goddess Pattini in Kerala and Sri Lanka.

steps.title: Taken by the sea
steps.text: The Buddhist epic Manimekalai, a sequel to the Tale of the Anklet, ends with Puhar swallowed by the sea after a king neglects the festival of Indra. Offshore surveys near Poompuhar have found submerged structures, but their age and meaning are debated. The poem’s heroine, Kovalan’s daughter, becomes a Buddhist nun.
steps.today: Today: Poompuhar’s coast, where the Kaveri meets the Bay of Bengal.

steps.title: The Kalabhra interval
steps.text: After the Sangam age the old kings fade from the record. A Pandya copper-plate grant of the 8th century says a Kalabhra king overran the land and took back gifts to Brahmins, until the Pandya Kadungon drove them out, about 590. Who the Kalabhras were is unknown. In the north, the Pallavas of Kanchipuram rose.
steps.today: Today: the Velvikudi copper plates are in the Government Museum, Chennai.

steps.title: Palm leaves into print
steps.text: By the 19th century the Sangam poems survived only on crumbling palm-leaf manuscripts. C. W. Damodaram Pillai printed some from 1887, and U. V. Swaminatha Iyer, searching houses and monasteries across the Tamil country, printed others, among them the Ten Long Poems in 1889, the Tale of the Anklet in 1892 and the Purananuru in 1894.
steps.today: Today: the U. V. Swaminatha Iyer Library, Besant Nagar, Chennai.

steps.title: A classical language
steps.text: In 2004 India declared Tamil its first classical language, citing its ancient literature. The Sangam poems are taught in schools and translated worldwide, and the Chola tiger, Pandya fish and Chera bow live on as emblems. Digs at Keezhadi, Adichanallur and Pattanam continue, and the Keeladi Museum opened in 2023.
steps.today: Today: Tamil is spoken by over 80 million people, in India, Sri Lanka and beyond.

items.name: Megasthenes
items.role: Greek envoy to the Maurya court
items.text: Sent by Seleucus to Chandragupta’s court at Pataliputra, Megasthenes wrote the Indica, now lost and known only from quotations by later writers such as Arrian and Strabo. His account mixes what he saw with what he was told, including the legend of Pandaia, the earliest foreign mention of a Pandya kingdom.

items.name: Ashoka
items.text: Ashoka ruled most of the subcontinent but never the far south. His edicts, carved on rocks and pillars, name the Tamil kingdoms as neighbours, and his minor rock edicts reach as far south as Karnataka. They are the oldest written record to name the Cholas, Pandyas and Keralaputras.

items.name: Elara (Ellalan)
items.text: The Mahavamsa remembers Elara as a just ruler, though not a Buddhist. The chronicle tells that he had his own son executed for running over a calf with his chariot. His defeat by Dutugamunu is the chronicle’s great set piece; it says Dutugamunu honoured Elara’s memory.

items.name: Kharavela
items.text: Kharavela is known almost only from his own inscription in the Elephant Cave at Udayagiri, which records his deeds year by year: wars to the west and north, gifts to Jain monks, and his campaign against the league of Tamil states. It is damaged, and scholars read parts of it differently.

items.name: Karikala
items.text: Karikala, ‘the charred leg’, a name later tradition explains by a fire he escaped as a boy, is the greatest Chola of the Sangam poems. He wins at Venni, rules from Uraiyur and Puhar, and is praised for clearing forests and taming the Kaveri. Much told of him comes from later sources and is tradition.

items.name: Nedunjeliyan
items.text: The poems praise this Pandya king for winning at Talaiyalanganam while still a youth. He was a poet himself: one poem in the Purananuru is in his name. The name Nedunjeliyan was borne by more than one Pandya, and which one the Mangulam inscription means is debated.

items.name: Avvaiyar
items.text: Some 59 Sangam poems are credited to Avvaiyar, among the best known of the poets, many of them on her patron Athiyaman. The name was borne by later poets too, including the author of short moral verses still taught to children, and tradition often blends them into one wise old woman.

items.name: Athiyaman Neduman Anji
items.text: Athiyaman was one of the famed generous chiefs (vallal) of the poems, ruling from Tagadur, today’s Dharmapuri. The Jambai inscription, found in 1981, names him as a Satiyaputra, linking the poems to Ashoka’s edict. Avvaiyar’s laments mourn his death.

items.name: Pliny the Elder
items.text: Pliny’s Natural History, an encyclopedia in 37 books, describes the sea route to India and grumbles about the gold it costs Rome. He died at Misenum trying to rescue people from the eruption of Vesuvius in 79 CE.

items.name: Mortimer Wheeler
items.text: As Director-General of the Archaeological Survey of India from 1944, Wheeler dug at Arikamedu in 1945, using Roman pottery to date Indian layers for the first time. He trained a generation of Indian archaeologists. Later work by Vimala Begley showed the site began before Roman contact.

items.name: Ilango Adigal
items.role: Poet of the Tale of the Anklet, in tradition
items.text: Tradition says Ilango was a Chera prince, the younger brother of King Senguttuvan, who became a monk so as not to stand in the way of his brother’s rule. His epic follows Kannagi across all three kingdoms, from Puhar to Madurai to the Chera hills. Its date and author are debated.

items.name: U. V. Swaminatha Iyer
items.text: A teacher at Kumbakonam and later Madras, Swaminatha Iyer spent decades tracking down palm-leaf manuscripts and comparing copies to print the classics accurately. He edited over 90 books, and is remembered as the grandfather of Tamil (Tamil Thatha).
